screens.title: OSPF Fundamentals and Single-Area Implementation
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll build a deep, practical understanding of Open Shortest Path First — OSPF — and why it's the preferred link-state Interior Gateway Protocol in many enterprise networks. You will learn how OSPF routers exchange compact link-state advertisements to construct an identical link-state database, and how each router uses Dijkstra's SPF algorithm on that database to compute loop-free shortest paths. We'll also cover the five OSPF packet types that drive neighbor discovery and reliable LSA flooding, the seven-state adjacency process that guarantees correct synchronization, and the configuration steps required to run single-area OSPF on Cisco IOS, including an important best practice: adjusting the auto-cost reference-bandwidth for high-speed links. Along the way you'll verify operation with the essential show commands and perform a simple hands-on exercise to see how a hello-interval mismatch affects adjacency. By the end you'll not only be able to configure OSPF area 0 and set router IDs, but you'll also be able to explain why OSPF's map-based approach scales and converges faster than distance-vector alternatives. Keep an eye out for common misconceptions, like confusing subnet masks and wildcard masks, and you'll be ready to reason about OSPF behavior in real networks.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › OSPF Fundamentals
Open Shortest Path First (OSPF)
Link-state IGP, fast convergence, hierarchical design, and precise path control.
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

OSPF routers share Link-State Advertisements to build an identical Link-State Database. Each router runs the Dijkstra Shortest Path First algorithm on that database to derive loop-free routes. In practice this means routers have an accurate map of the area and compute best paths independently, which improves convergence and scalability compared with distance-vector approaches.

You'll configure single-area OSPF on Cisco IOS, tune reference bandwidth for high-speed links, and verify operation using the key show commands.

In this lesson
LSA, LSDB, SPF
How topology information is advertised and used to calculate routes.
Coming up
OSPF Packets & States
Hello, DBD, LSR, LSU, LSAck and the seven adjacency states.
Why this matters
Stable, scalable routing
OSPF's map-based approach reduces loops and enables predictable path selection.
Core concept cards
Link-State Advertisement (LSA)
Small packets describing a router's links and interface states; they are flooded within an area.
Link-State Database (LSDB)
The synchronized collection of LSAs every router in an area keeps.
SPF / Cost
Routers compute shortest path trees using link costs derived from bandwidth.
Explore Key Topics: Link-state vs Distance Vector, OSPF packet types, single-area configuration and verification.

Second, you'll describe the three core components — LSAs, the Link-State Database, and the SPF algorithm — and why they form a consistent, loop-free routing foundation. Third, you'll identify the five OSPF packet types and explain their roles: Hello for discovery and DR election, Database Description to summarize LSDB contents, Link-State Request to fetch missing LSAs, Link-State Update to carry LSAs, and Link-State Acknowledgment to ensure reliable flooding. screens.title: Link-State vs Distance Vector
screens.narratorSegment: Begin with a precise definition: distance-vector protocols share reachability and distance to destinations with neighbors only. In contrast, link-state protocols like OSPF flood link-state advertisements containing link, interface, and neighbor information so every router builds a complete area topology. This difference matters because link-state routers run the Dijkstra SPF algorithm on the identical LSDB to compute a shortest-path tree, producing loop-free paths without relying on incremental route updates. A concrete example: with RIP a router learns routes hop-by-hop and may slowly propagate changes; with OSPF, a single LSA flood informs all routers of a topology change and each recalculates routes locally, which improves convergence time. Common misconception: link-state is not stateless — routers still maintain state, but it is the synchronized LSDB, not only neighbor distances. Another pitfall is thinking OSPF removes administrative control; in fact OSPF cost and reference-bandwidth let you shape path selection. Key takeaway: link-state gives you a consistent map and predictable SPF-based path selection; ask yourself which failure scenarios require coordinated LSDB updates rather than just neighbor reachability checks. Link-State vs Distance Vector means link-state routers flood lsas to build a shared topology map; distance-vector routers exchange neighbor distances only.. In practical terms, how ospf's map-based approach differs from distance-vector routing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › Link-State vs Distance Vector
Definition and contrast
Clear, practical differences and an example to ground your understanding.
Distance-Vector (example: RIP)
  • Routers share routing tables with neighbors only.
  • Convergence depends on incremental updates and timers.
Link-State (example: OSPF)
  • Routers flood LSAs; each builds an LSDB representing the area.
  • Each router runs SPF to compute shortest path trees locally.
Concrete example
A single link failure produces an LSA flood in OSPF so all routers can immediately recompute paths; ripple effects in distance-vector protocols are slower and can produce loops without split-horizon or hold-downs.
Key Takeaway

Link-state provides a synchronized topology map and deterministic SPF computation, enabling faster, loop-free convergence compared to distance-vector methods.

Visual analogy
Think of distance-vector as many people gossiping only with neighbors, while link-state is everyone posting a map to a shared board. With the board everyone can compute the best route from the same authoritative source.
Common misconception
Assuming link-state automatically chooses higher-bandwidth links—OSPF uses configurable cost derived from bandwidth; you should tune reference-bandwidth for very high-speed links.
Check your understanding
If two routers in an area have different LSDB contents, will SPF produce the same routes? Why or why not?

screens.title: LSAs, LSDB, and SPF workflow
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the OSPF topology workflow step by step. First, each router generates LSAs describing directly connected links, interface states, and reachable networks. These LSAs are flooded reliably within the OSPF area using Link-State Update packets, and receipt is confirmed with Link-State Acknowledgment packets to ensure every router eventually sees each LSA. Second, all LSAs are stored in the Link-State Database; within an area every router aims to have an identical LSDB. Third, once the LSDB is current, each router runs the Dijkstra Shortest Path First algorithm over the topology to build a shortest-path tree rooted at itself; the calculated tree yields the next-hop and outgoing interface for each destination. Concrete example: when a router's interface goes down, it emits a new Router LSA; neighbors flood that LSA and once the flood completes, each router recalculates SPF to avoid the failed link. Misconception: flooding is not broadcast chaos — LSA flooding follows sequence numbers and acknowledgments to guarantee reliable, loop-free propagation. Final takeaway: think of OSPF as advertise, flood, store, compute — that sequence is the core of its fast, consistent convergence.

keyIdea.title: Process highlight
keyIdea.text: Advertise local state (LSA), flood reliably, keep identical LSDBs, run SPF to compute the shortest-path tree.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › LSA → LSDB → SPF
OSPF topology workflow
1. Generate LSA
Router describes directly connected interfaces and links. Router LSAs are Type 1 LSAs on normal areas.
→
2. Flood & reliable delivery
LSUs carry LSAs and LSAcks confirm receipt so flooding is reliable and ordered.
→
3. Store in LSDB
All routers in an area aim to have an identical LSDB collection of LSAs.
4. Run SPF
Dijkstra's algorithm constructs the shortest-path tree using LSDB link costs. The root is the calculating router and the tree produces the routing decisions.
Example scenario
Router A's interface to a switch goes down. Router A issues a new Router LSA; neighbors flood the update, ack it, and everyone runs SPF. Routes that used the failed link are recalculated immediately.
Misconception check
LSA flooding is not uncontrolled. Sequence numbers and acknowledgements prevent duplicate or out-of-order topology application.
Process cards
  1. LSA generation — advertise local state.
  2. Flooding — LSU and LSAck ensure reliability.
  3. LSDB consistency — identical view per area.
  4. SPF run — compute shortest-path tree.
Key Takeaway

OSPF's advertise‑flood‑store‑compute sequence gives fast, consistent convergence across an area.

screens.title: OSPF Cost and Reference Bandwidth
screens.narratorSegment: OSPF uses a cost metric derived from link bandwidth. By default Cisco IOS computes cost as 100,000,000 divided by the link bandwidth in bits per second. Concretely this means a Fast Ethernet 100 Mbps link gets a cost of 1 using the 100 megabit reference, and a Gigabit link also often reports a cost of 1 unless you adjust the reference bandwidth. This can lead to unintended equal-costs on very high-speed links. The practical remedy is the auto-cost reference-bandwidth command under the OSPF process to increase the reference to a value that reflects your fastest links, for example 10000 for 10 Gbps. Example configuration shows router ospf 1, network statements with wildcard masks, setting router-id, and auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000. A common misconception is changing the reference bandwidth at one router alone will fix costs — the reference affects local cost calculation, so change it consistently across the area to keep path selection predictable. Key takeaway: tune reference bandwidth so link costs reflect relative bandwidth differences you expect routers to prefer. OSPF Cost and Reference Bandwidth means default ospf cost = 10^8 / bandwidth (bps); adjust reference-bandwidth to reflect high-speed links and preserve meaningful costs.. In practical terms, how ospf computes link cost and why you must adjust reference bandwidth. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.text: Default OSPF cost = 10^8 / bandwidth (bps); adjust reference-bandwidth to reflect high-speed links and preserve meaningful costs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › OSPF Cost
OSPF cost calculation
Understand the formula and how to adjust reference bandwidth to get meaningful costs across high-speed links.
Cost formula
OSPF cost = 10^8 / bandwidth(in bps). Using default reference, both 100 Mbps and 1 Gbps links can show equal cost unless you change the reference.
Why change reference-bandwidth
Adjusting auto-cost reference-bandwidth ensures the cost reflects relative differences between 1Gbps, 10Gbps, and faster links, avoiding unwanted equal-costs.
Key Takeaway

Set reference-bandwidth consistently across the area to produce meaningful, predictable OSPF costs for path selection.

router ospf 1          ! '1' is the OSPF process ID, local to the router
 network 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255 area 0 ! Wildcard mask and Area ID
 network 10.0.0.0 0.255.255.255 area 0
 auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000 ! Adjust for 10 Gbps links
 router-id 1.1.1.1      ! Manually set router ID
Concrete example
If you leave the default reference, a 100 Mbps and a 1 Gbps link may both compute cost 1, hiding the advantage of the faster link. Setting reference-bandwidth to 10000 makes the 1 Gbps cost smaller than a 100 Mbps link.

screens.title: The Five OSPF Packet Types
screens.narratorSegment: OSPF uses five packet types that together create a reliable synchronization protocol. Hello packets establish neighbor relationships and elect a Designated Router and Backup Designated Router on multi-access networks; they are sent periodically to maintain adjacency. Database Description, or DBD, packets summarize the contents of a neighbor's LSDB so peers can quickly compare what they know; after Hellos, neighbors exchange DBDs to identify missing or stale LSAs. If a router finds missing LSAs, it sends Link-State Request packets to fetch them. The neighbor responds with a Link-State Update containing the requested LSAs; LSUs are the vehicle for flooding actual topology information. Finally, Link-State Acknowledgment packets confirm receipt of LSUs so flooding is reliable. A common misconception is that DBDs contain full LSAs — they only summarize. Concrete scenario: two routers on a LAN exchange Hellos, elect a DR/BDR, send DBDs to compare LSDBs, one sends an LSR for missing LSAs, and the other replies with an LSU and expects an LSAck. This five-step choreography ensures accurate LSDB synchronization and reliable flooding. The Five OSPF Packet Types means hello: discover; dbd: summarize db; lsr: request; lsu: update/flood; lsack: acknowledge — together they guarantee lsdb sync and reliable flooding.. In practical terms, what each packet type does and when it's used. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.5 › OSPF Packet Types
Five OSPF packet types
Learn what each packet does and a quick example of use in adjacency formation and LSDB synchronization.
Hello (Type 1)
Used for neighbor discovery, adjacency maintenance, and DR/BDR election. Sent periodically on OSPF-enabled interfaces.
Database Description (Type 2)
Summarizes the sender's LSDB contents so peers can detect missing or out-of-date LSAs.
Link-State Request (Type 3)
Requests specific LSAs that a router lacks, identified after comparing DBDs.
Link-State Update (Type 4)
Carries one or more LSAs and is used to flood topology information throughout the area.
Link-State Acknowledgment (Type 5)
Acknowledges receipt of LSUs to ensure reliable LSA flooding; can be explicit or implicit depending on transport.
Example choreography
Two neighbors exchange Hellos, send DBDs to compare LSDBs, one issues LSRs for missing LSAs, the other replies with LSUs, and the receiver sends LSAcks to confirm.
Key Takeaway

These five packet types together provide discovery, summary, request, delivery, and acknowledgement — the essential mechanics for consistent LSDBs.

screens.title: OSPF Neighbor Discovery and the Seven States
screens.narratorSegment: OSPF adjacency formation progresses through a defined sequence of states that ensure correctness before full synchronization. It begins in the Down state where no Hello has been seen. When a Hello arrives the neighbor moves to Init indicating one-way communication. On multi-access networks, the 2-Way state is reached when bi-directional Hellos are observed; during 2-Way the DR and BDR election occurs. If neighbors decide to form a full adjacency they enter ExStart to negotiate master/slave roles and initial sequence numbers, then Exchange where DBD packets are sent to compare LSDB summaries. During Loading, routers send LSRs for any missing LSAs and receive LSUs in reply. Finally, the Full state indicates complete LSDB synchronization and ongoing LSA exchange. Concrete example: two routers on a point-to-point link typically progress rapidly to Full because no DR/BDR election is needed. A common misconception is blaming area mismatch for a 2-Way stall: on multi-access links a failed DR/BDR election or misconfigured priority often explains 2-Way stalls. Takeaway: use show ip ospf neighbor to map observed states to precise troubleshooting actions. OSPF Neighbor Discovery and the Seven States means down → init → 2-way → exstart → exchange → loading → full — each state represents a clear step toward lsdb synchronization.. In practical terms, from down to full — what each state means and when it occurs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Adjacency Requirements and Common Mismatches
screens.narratorSegment: For two routers to form an OSPF adjacency they must agree on several interface and area parameters. The most common required matches are hello and dead intervals, area ID, authentication settings, stub area flags, and subnet mask on the link. If any of these parameters differ, adjacency may fail or stall at an intermediate state. Concrete example: if Router A uses the default hello of 10 seconds and Router B has an interface configured with hello-interval 10 while Router A was changed to 1, they will not form a stable adjacency and will likely stay in Init or drop to Down depending on timing. Another classic error is using a subnet mask instead of a wildcard mask in a network statement; that prevents interfaces from being enabled under OSPF as expected. Troubleshooting steps: first check show ip ospf neighbor to see the state, then show ip ospf interface to compare timers and area, and finally show ip interface brief and ip addresses to verify subnet alignment. Takeaway: methodically compare these parameters across peers to isolate adjacency issues quickly. Parameters that must match

Common misconfiguration
Using a subnet mask in the network command instead of a wildcard mask will prevent interfaces from being included in the OSPF process as intended.

  1. show ip ospf neighbor — observe neighbor state.
  2. show ip ospf interface — compare hello/dead, area, and auth.
  3. verify IP addressing and masks on both sides.

If hello intervals mismatch the neighbor will not remain in Full; adjusting the hello-interval on one interface to match the other restores adjacency after the timers realign.

A methodical parameter comparison using show commands is the fastest way to find why an OSPF adjacency fails.

Configuration steps
  1. Enable OSPF with router ospf <process-id>.
  2. Set router-id to a unique 32-bit value for stability.
  3. Add network statements with wildcard masks and area 0.
  4. Tune auto-cost reference-bandwidth if necessary.

Apply the network statements with the correct wildcard masks and set router-ids so OSPF areas remain stable and predictable.

screens.title: Verifying OSPF: Key show commands
screens.narratorSegment: Verifying OSPF relies on a small set of show commands that together provide a full operational picture. show ip ospf neighbor lists established adjacencies and their states — use it first to confirm whether neighbors reached Full. show ip ospf interface reports OSPF timers, area membership, and interface cost; it's where you compare hello and dead intervals or verify the calculated cost. show ip ospf database dumps the LSDB so you can inspect which LSAs are present and verify that expected Router and Network LSAs exist. Finally, show ip route ospf shows OSPF-learned routes installed in the routing table. A concrete verification workflow: after enabling OSPF, run show ip ospf neighbor to confirm Full state; if not Full, run show ip ospf interface to compare timers and area IDs; then check show ip ospf database to see whether peers' LSAs are present; and inspect show ip route ospf to confirm networks were learned. Misconception: seeing LSAs alone doesn't guarantee forwarding; always confirm that the route is installed in the routing table. Takeaway: these four commands together are your primary visibility tools for OSPF health and troubleshooting.

Command overview

Shows neighbor IDs, priority, state, and address. Use this first to see adjacency state.
show ip ospf interface
Shows timers, area, cost, and whether OSPF is enabled on the interface.

screens.title: Hands-on Activity: Hello Interval Mismatch
screens.narratorSegment: This guided activity helps you see how a simple timer mismatch affects OSPF adjacency. Start with the working topology: R1 and R2 configured in area 0, with router-ids and loopbacks configured. First verify adjacency with show ip ospf neighbor; ensure both routers show the neighbor in Full. Next change R1's Gigabit interface hello interval to 10 seconds using interface configuration mode and ip ospf hello-interval 10. Wait and observe on R2: execute show ip ospf neighbor and you should see the adjacency transition to a non-Full state or disappear depending on timing — this demonstrates that mismatched hello intervals prevent stable adjacency. Then restore the default hello or set R2 to match R1 and observe adjacency return to Full. A common misconception is that OSPF process ID mismatches cause hello problems — process IDs are local and do not affect neighbor interoperability. Key troubleshooting steps here are to compare show ip ospf interface timers and to check for dead timer expiration on the peer. This hands-on trial shows how precise timer alignment is essential for OSPF adjacency. screens.title: OSPF Best Practices for Single-Area Designs
screens.narratorSegment: When designing and operating single-area OSPF, a few best practices dramatically reduce surprises. First, always assign a static router-id for predictable LSA origin and stable identification in the LSDB. Second, use Area 0 as the backbone and keep the design simple in single-area deployments; area 0 is special and other areas must connect to it. Third, set auto-cost reference-bandwidth consistently across routers in the area so link cost comparisons are consistent and path selection behaves as you expect. Fourth, adopt a verification discipline: after configuration, run show ip ospf neighbor, show ip ospf interface, show ip ospf database, and show ip route ospf in that order to confirm adjacency, interface parameters, LSDB contents, and route installation. Concrete example: when adding a 10 Gbps link, updating the reference bandwidth across all routers ensures that the 10 Gbps link actually appears preferred in SPF calculations instead of unexpectedly being treated the same as slower links. A common mistake is changing the reference on only one router — do it consistently. Final takeaway: consistent IDs, consistent reference bandwidth, proper area placement, and a standard verification workflow are your recipe for reliable OSPF operation.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll build a deep, practical understanding of Open Shortest Path First — OSPF — and why it's the preferred link-state Interior Gateway Protocol in many enterprise networks. You will learn how OSPF routers exchange compact link-state advertisements to construct an identical link-state database, and how each router uses Dijkstra's SPF algorithm on that database to compute loop-free shortest paths. We'll also cover the five OSPF packet types that drive neighbor discovery and reliable LSA flooding, the seven-state adjacency process that guarantees correct synchronization, and the configuration steps required to run single-area OSPF on Cisco IOS, including an important best practice: adjusting the auto-cost reference-bandwidth for high-speed links. Along the way you'll verify operation with the essential show commands and perform a simple hands-on exercise to see how a hello-interval mismatch affects adjacency. By the end you'll not only be able to configure OSPF area 0 and set router IDs, but you'll also be able to explain why OSPF's map-based approach scales and converges faster than distance-vector alternatives. Keep an eye out for common misconceptions, like confusing subnet masks and wildcard masks, and you'll be ready to reason about OSPF behavior in real networks.

This first objectives slide focuses on core understanding you need to reason about OSPF. First, you will explain how link-state routing differs from distance-vector routing: rather than routing by rumor, link-state routers exchange LSAs to build a full topology map and then compute routes locally with Dijkstra's algorithm. Second, you'll describe the three core components — LSAs, the Link-State Database, and the SPF algorithm — and why they form a consistent, loop-free routing foundation. Third, you'll identify the five OSPF packet types and explain their roles: Hello for discovery and DR election, Database Description to summarize LSDB contents, Link-State Request to fetch missing LSAs, Link-State Update to carry LSAs, and Link-State Acknowledgment to ensure reliable flooding. Fourth, you'll gain the ability to configure basic single-area OSPF on Cisco IOS using process, network statements, router-id, and reference-bandwidth commands. In practice these skills let you design predictable routing behavior, verify correct adjacencies, and avoid common setup errors like using a subnet mask instead of a wildcard mask. Which objective feels most critical for your current tasks?

This second objectives slide focuses on operational skills and troubleshooting. First, you'll understand OSPF neighbor discovery and the seven adjacency states from Down to Full, and you'll be able to explain why a router stops at a particular state. Second, you'll learn the precise interface and area parameters that must match for neighbor adjacency: hello/dead intervals, area ID, authentication, stub flags, and subnet relationships. Third, you'll practice verifying OSPF with the essential show commands: show ip ospf neighbor, show ip ospf interface, show ip ospf database, and show ip route ospf. These commands give you visibility into adjacency formation, interface timers, the LSDB contents, and learned routes. Fourth, you'll learn a focused troubleshooting workflow for common faults, such as hello interval mismatches or missing network statements, and practice an exercise where an intentional hello-interval change causes adjacency loss then is corrected. Together these skills let you diagnose and repair OSPF adjacency and LSDB synchronization issues quickly in a production environment.

Begin with a precise definition: distance-vector protocols share reachability and distance to destinations with neighbors only. In contrast, link-state protocols like OSPF flood link-state advertisements containing link, interface, and neighbor information so every router builds a complete area topology. This difference matters because link-state routers run the Dijkstra SPF algorithm on the identical LSDB to compute a shortest-path tree, producing loop-free paths without relying on incremental route updates. A concrete example: with RIP a router learns routes hop-by-hop and may slowly propagate changes; with OSPF, a single LSA flood informs all routers of a topology change and each recalculates routes locally, which improves convergence time. Common misconception: link-state is not stateless — routers still maintain state, but it is the synchronized LSDB, not only neighbor distances. Another pitfall is thinking OSPF removes administrative control; in fact OSPF cost and reference-bandwidth let you shape path selection. Key takeaway: link-state gives you a consistent map and predictable SPF-based path selection; ask yourself which failure scenarios require coordinated LSDB updates rather than just neighbor reachability checks. Let's walk through the OSPF topology workflow step by step. First, each router generates LSAs describing directly connected links, interface states, and reachable networks. These LSAs are flooded reliably within the OSPF area using Link-State Update packets, and receipt is confirmed with Link-State Acknowledgment packets to ensure every router eventually sees each LSA. Second, all LSAs are stored in the Link-State Database; within an area every router aims to have an identical LSDB. Third, once the LSDB is current, each router runs the Dijkstra Shortest Path First algorithm over the topology to build a shortest-path tree rooted at itself; the calculated tree yields the next-hop and outgoing interface for each destination. Concrete example: when a router's interface goes down, it emits a new Router LSA; neighbors flood that LSA and once the flood completes, each router recalculates SPF to avoid the failed link. Misconception: flooding is not broadcast chaos — LSA flooding follows sequence numbers and acknowledgments to guarantee reliable, loop-free propagation. Final takeaway: think of OSPF as advertise, flood, store, compute — that sequence is the core of its fast, consistent convergence.

OSPF uses a cost metric derived from link bandwidth. By default Cisco IOS computes cost as 100,000,000 divided by the link bandwidth in bits per second. Concretely this means a Fast Ethernet 100 Mbps link gets a cost of 1 using the 100 megabit reference, and a Gigabit link also often reports a cost of 1 unless you adjust the reference bandwidth. This can lead to unintended equal-costs on very high-speed links. The practical remedy is the auto-cost reference-bandwidth command under the OSPF process to increase the reference to a value that reflects your fastest links, for example 10000 for 10 Gbps. Example configuration shows router ospf 1, network statements with wildcard masks, setting router-id, and auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000. A common misconception is changing the reference bandwidth at one router alone will fix costs — the reference affects local cost calculation, so change it consistently across the area to keep path selection predictable. Key takeaway: tune reference bandwidth so link costs reflect relative bandwidth differences you expect routers to prefer. OSPF uses five packet types that together create a reliable synchronization protocol. Hello packets establish neighbor relationships and elect a Designated Router and Backup Designated Router on multi-access networks; they are sent periodically to maintain adjacency. Database Description, or DBD, packets summarize the contents of a neighbor's LSDB so peers can quickly compare what they know; after Hellos, neighbors exchange DBDs to identify missing or stale LSAs. If a router finds missing LSAs, it sends Link-State Request packets to fetch them. The neighbor responds with a Link-State Update containing the requested LSAs; LSUs are the vehicle for flooding actual topology information. Finally, Link-State Acknowledgment packets confirm receipt of LSUs so flooding is reliable. A common misconception is that DBDs contain full LSAs — they only summarize. Concrete scenario: two routers on a LAN exchange Hellos, elect a DR/BDR, send DBDs to compare LSDBs, one sends an LSR for missing LSAs, and the other replies with an LSU and expects an LSAck. This five-step choreography ensures accurate LSDB synchronization and reliable flooding. OSPF adjacency formation progresses through a defined sequence of states that ensure correctness before full synchronization. It begins in the Down state where no Hello has been seen. When a Hello arrives the neighbor moves to Init indicating one-way communication. On multi-access networks, the 2-Way state is reached when bi-directional Hellos are observed; during 2-Way the DR and BDR election occurs. If neighbors decide to form a full adjacency they enter ExStart to negotiate master/slave roles and initial sequence numbers, then Exchange where DBD packets are sent to compare LSDB summaries. During Loading, routers send LSRs for any missing LSAs and receive LSUs in reply. Finally, the Full state indicates complete LSDB synchronization and ongoing LSA exchange. Concrete example: two routers on a point-to-point link typically progress rapidly to Full because no DR/BDR election is needed. A common misconception is blaming area mismatch for a 2-Way stall: on multi-access links a failed DR/BDR election or misconfigured priority often explains 2-Way stalls. Takeaway: use show ip ospf neighbor to map observed states to precise troubleshooting actions. For two routers to form an OSPF adjacency they must agree on several interface and area parameters. The most common required matches are hello and dead intervals, area ID, authentication settings, stub area flags, and subnet mask on the link. If any of these parameters differ, adjacency may fail or stall at an intermediate state. Concrete example: if Router A uses the default hello of 10 seconds and Router B has an interface configured with hello-interval 10 while Router A was changed to 1, they will not form a stable adjacency and will likely stay in Init or drop to Down depending on timing. Another classic error is using a subnet mask instead of a wildcard mask in a network statement; that prevents interfaces from being enabled under OSPF as expected. Troubleshooting steps: first check show ip ospf neighbor to see the state, then show ip ospf interface to compare timers and area, and finally show ip interface brief and ip addresses to verify subnet alignment. Takeaway: methodically compare these parameters across peers to isolate adjacency issues quickly. Verifying OSPF relies on a small set of show commands that together provide a full operational picture. show ip ospf neighbor lists established adjacencies and their states — use it first to confirm whether neighbors reached Full. show ip ospf interface reports OSPF timers, area membership, and interface cost; it's where you compare hello and dead intervals or verify the calculated cost. show ip ospf database dumps the LSDB so you can inspect which LSAs are present and verify that expected Router and Network LSAs exist. Finally, show ip route ospf shows OSPF-learned routes installed in the routing table. A concrete verification workflow: after enabling OSPF, run show ip ospf neighbor to confirm Full state; if not Full, run show ip ospf interface to compare timers and area IDs; then check show ip ospf database to see whether peers' LSAs are present; and inspect show ip route ospf to confirm networks were learned. Misconception: seeing LSAs alone doesn't guarantee forwarding; always confirm that the route is installed in the routing table. Takeaway: these four commands together are your primary visibility tools for OSPF health and troubleshooting.

When designing and operating single-area OSPF, a few best practices dramatically reduce surprises. First, always assign a static router-id for predictable LSA origin and stable identification in the LSDB. Second, use Area 0 as the backbone and keep the design simple in single-area deployments; area 0 is special and other areas must connect to it. Third, set auto-cost reference-bandwidth consistently across routers in the area so link cost comparisons are consistent and path selection behaves as you expect. Fourth, adopt a verification discipline: after configuration, run show ip ospf neighbor, show ip ospf interface, show ip ospf database, and show ip route ospf in that order to confirm adjacency, interface parameters, LSDB contents, and route installation. Concrete example: when adding a 10 Gbps link, updating the reference bandwidth across all routers ensures that the 10 Gbps link actually appears preferred in SPF calculations instead of unexpectedly being treated the same as slower links. A common mistake is changing the reference on only one router — do it consistently. Final takeaway: consistent IDs, consistent reference bandwidth, proper area placement, and a standard verification workflow are your recipe for reliable OSPF operation.
